results.title: Projective special linear group
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a natural number $n$ and a field $F$, $\mathrm{PSL}_n(F)$ is the quotient $\mathrm{SL}_n(F)/Z(\mathrm{SL}_n(F))$ of the special linear group $\mathrm{SL}_n(F)$ of $n \times n$ matrices over $F$ with determinant $1$ by its centre.

results.title: Kourovka 14.60: new element orders in extensions of projective special linear groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that for every $n \ge 3$, every prime $p$ and every $k \ge 1$, with $q = p^k$ and $\mathbb{F}_q$ the field with $q$ elements, the following holds: whenever $H$ is a nontrivial normal subgroup of a finite group $G$ and $G/H$ is isomorphic to the projective special linear group $\mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$, some element of $G$ has an order that is not the order of any element of $G/H$.

results.title: Extensions of PSL have a new element order

results.title: Degree of a function in the Selberg class
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a function $F$ in the Selberg class whose functional equation has Gamma-factor scalings $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r$, the degree of $F$ is $d_F = 2 \sum_{j=1}^{r} \lambda_j$.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the degree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a function in the Selberg class with Gamma-factor scalings $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r$. Then the degree $d_F = 2 \sum_{j=1}^{r} \lambda_j$ satisfies $d_F \ge 0$.

results.title: Holomorphy of Selberg class functions away from $s = 1$

results.summary: For a function $F$ in the Selberg class, $F$ is complex differentiable at every $s \in \mathbb{C}$ with $s \ne 1$.

results.title: Residues that are squares modulo $2^{2k-1}$ but not modulo $2^{2k}$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k \ge 0$ and let $x$ be an integer with $0 \le x < 2^{2k}$, where the exponents $2k - 1$ and $2k - 2$ are truncated at $0$. Then $x$ is a square modulo $2^{2k-1}$ but not a square modulo $2^{2k}$ if and only if $x = 2^{2k-1}$ or $x = 2^{2k-1} + 2^{2k-2}$.

results.title: The partition function $c_2$ of Nyirenda and Mugwangwavari
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an integer $n \ge 0$, $c_2(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ for which there is an integer $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$ such that $j$ appears exactly $j$ times, every part other than $j$ is at least $2j + 1$, and every even part that is at least $2j + 2$ appears only once.

reading_title.source: The partition function $c_2$ of Nyirenda and Mugwangwavari

results.title: The initial-repetitions partition function $c_3$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \ge 0$, $c_3(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ for which there is an integer $j$ with $1 \le j \le n$ such that the part $1$ appears exactly $j^2$ or $j^2 + 1$ times, every odd part larger than $1$ appears exactly once, every even part appears exactly once, and every even part greater than $2j$ is at least $4j + 4$ and divisible by $4$.

reading_title.source: The initial-repetitions partition function $c_3$

results.title: The partition function $c_8$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \ge 0$, $c_8(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ such that either (a) all parts are even and distinct, or (b) for some positive integer $j$, the largest odd part is $2j - 1$, every positive odd integer $i \le j$ appears once or twice, every odd integer $i$ with $j < i \le 2j - 1$ appears exactly once, all even parts are distinct, and every even part greater than $j$ is at least $2j + 2$.

results.title: The initial-repetitions partition function $c_8'$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $n \ge 0$, $c_8'(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ into distinct even parts plus the sum, over $m = 1, \dots, n$, of the number of partitions of $n$ in which every even number $2i$ with $1 \le i \le m$ is a part, every even part at most $m$ appears at most twice, every odd part at most $m$ appears exactly once, and every part greater than $m$ is even and appears exactly once.

results.title: Tight family of probability measures
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a space carrying a σ-algebra and a topology. A family $(\mu_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of probability measures on $\alpha$ is tight if its range $\{\mu_i : i \in \iota\}$ is a tight set of measures: for every $\varepsilon \in (0, \infty]$ there is a compact set $K \subseteq \alpha$ such that $\mu_i(\alpha \setminus K) \le \varepsilon$ for every index $i$.

results.title: Tightness on the real line
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A family $(\mu_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$ is tight in the real-line sense if for every $\varepsilon \in (0, \infty]$ there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\mu_i([-M, M]) \ge 1 - \varepsilon$ for every index $i$.

results.title: Existence conjecture for Steiner systems
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for all natural numbers $r < k$ there is an $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$ with $\binom{k-i}{r-i} \mid \binom{n-i}{r-i}$ for all $0 \le i < r$, there is a Steiner system $S(r, k, n)$: a family $F$ of $k$-element subsets of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that every $r$-element subset of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is contained in exactly one member of $F$ (Erdős Problem 722).

results.title: Generalized Johnson graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $v$, $k$ and $i$, the generalized Johnson graph $J(v,k,i)$ is the graph whose vertices are the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, v-1\}$, in which two distinct vertices are adjacent if and only if their intersection has exactly $i$ elements.

results.title: Johnson graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$, the Johnson graph $J(n, k)$ has as vertices the $k$-element subsets of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, and two vertices $s$ and $t$ are adjacent when $|s \cap t| + 1 = k$, that is, when $s$ and $t$ share exactly $k - 1$ elements.

results.title: Adjacency in the Johnson graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and $k$-element subsets $s$ and $t$ of $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$, the vertices $s$ and $t$ of the Johnson graph $J(n, k)$ are adjacent if and only if $|s \cap t| + 1 = k$.

results.title: Instances of GRAPH COLORING
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of GRAPH COLORING is a triple $(n, E, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the edges, and a natural number $K$, the bound on the number of colors.

results.title: Graph of a GRAPH COLORING instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The graph of an instance $(n, E, K)$ of GRAPH COLORING is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

results.title: Well-formed GRAPH COLORING instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of GRAPH COLORING is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$.

results.title: Feasible GRAPH COLORING instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, K)$ of GRAPH COLORING is feasible when its graph is $K$-colorable, that is, when its vertices can be assigned colors from $\{0, \dots, K - 1\}$ so that adjacent vertices receive different colors.

results.title: GRAPH COLORING as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem GRAPH COLORING accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an instance of GRAPH COLORING that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

results.title: GRAPH COLORING is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem GRAPH COLORING belongs to NP, and every decision problem $L$ in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to GRAPH COLORING.

results.title: Trie
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A trie with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$ is a node consisting of an optional value in $\beta$ and a finite list of children, each child being a pair of a letter in $\alpha$ and a trie. The letters labelling the children need not be distinct.

results.title: Empty trie
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty trie is the trie consisting of a single root node that stores no value and has no children, so it contains no key-value entries.

results.title: Trie lookup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The lookup of a key (a list over $\alpha$) in a trie returns an optional value in $\beta$, by recursion on the key. For the empty key it is the optional value stored at the root. For a key with first letter $a$ followed by the key $k$, it fails if no child of the root is labelled $a$, and otherwise it is the lookup of $k$ in the first child labelled $a$.

results.title: Trie insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Inserting a value $v$ at a key $k$ (a list of letters) in a trie stores $v$ at the node reached by following $k$ from the root, replacing any value stored there. Along the way, a missing child is created as an empty trie and appended after its siblings, an existing child is updated in place, and all other values and children are unchanged.

results.title: Valid trie
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Validity of tries is defined inductively: a trie node with optional value $v$ and child list $c$ is valid when the letters labelling the children in $c$ are pairwise distinct and every child trie in $c$ is valid.

results.title: Entries of a trie
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The entries of a trie are the list of its key-value pairs, where a key is a list of letters. If the root stores a value $v$, the list begins with the pair consisting of the empty key and $v$; it continues, for each child in the stored sibling order, with the entries $(k, w)$ of that child, in order, each rewritten as $(a k, w)$, where $a$ is the letter labelling the child and $a k$ is the key $k$ with $a$ prepended.

results.title: Lookup in the empty trie
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the empty trie returns no value.

results.title: Lookup after insertion in a trie
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with decidable equality. For every trie $T$ with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, every key $k$ and every value $v \in \beta$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $T$ by inserting $v$ at $k$ returns $v$.

results.title: Trie insertion leaves other keys unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every trie $T$, all keys $k \ne k'$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k'$ in $T$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $T$.

results.title: Valid trie nodes have distinct child keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a trie node with optional value $v$ and child list $c$ is valid, then the letters labelling the children in $c$ are pairwise distinct.

results.title: Validity of the empty trie
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The empty trie is valid.

results.title: Insertion preserves trie validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a trie $T$ is valid, then for every key $k$ (a list of letters) and every value $v$, the trie obtained by inserting $v$ at $k$ in $T$ is valid.

results.title: Trie lookup agrees with the entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every valid trie $T$, every key $k$ and every value $v$, looking up $k$ in $T$ returns $v$ if and only if $(k, v)$ is one of the entries of $T$.

results.title: Lookup equivalence of tries
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two tries $T$ and $T'$ are lookup-equivalent when, for every key $k$, looking up $k$ in $T$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $T'$.

results.title: Reflexivity of trie lookup equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every trie is lookup-equivalent to itself.

results.title: Symmetry of trie lookup equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a trie $T$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T'$, then $T'$ is lookup-equivalent to $T$.

results.title: Transitivity of trie lookup equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a trie $T_1$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T_2$ and $T_2$ is lookup-equivalent to a trie $T_3$, then $T_1$ is lookup-equivalent to $T_3$.

results.title: Lookup-equivalent valid tries have the same entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ and $T'$ be valid tries with keys that are lists over $\alpha$ and values in $\beta$, and suppose $T$ and $T'$ are lookup-equivalent. Then for every key $k$ and every value $v \in \beta$, the pair $(k, v)$ occurs in the entry list of $T$ if and only if it occurs in the entry list of $T'$.

results.title: Insertions at distinct keys commute in a trie
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every trie $T$, all keys $k_1 \ne k_2$ and all values $v_1, v_2$, inserting $v_1$ at $k_1$ and then $v_2$ at $k_2$ gives a trie that is lookup-equivalent to the one obtained by inserting $v_2$ at $k_2$ and then $v_1$ at $k_1$.

results.title: Empty trie nodes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty-node test is true on a trie node exactly when the node carries no value and has no children; when deletion leaves a child in this state, the child is removed from its parent.

results.title: Characterization of empty nodes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The empty-node test is true on a trie $t$ exactly when $t$ is the node with no value and no children, that is, the empty trie.

results.title: Setting a child in a trie's child list

Setting the child at $a$ to $t$ in $L$ gives the following list. If no entry of $L$ has key $a$, the result is $L$ itself when $t$ is empty, and $L$ with $(a, t)$ appended at the end otherwise. results.title: Looking up a child just set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie pairs, $a$ a letter and $c$ a trie, and let $L'$ be obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children). Looking up $a$ in $L'$ finds nothing when $c$ has neither value nor children, and finds $c$ otherwise.

results.title: Setting a child leaves the other children unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie pairs, $c$ a trie and $a \ne b$ letters, and let $L'$ be obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $b$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $b$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children). Then looking up $a$ in $L'$ gives the same result as looking up $a$ in $L$.

results.title: Setting a child preserves the child-list part of validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of letter–trie pairs whose letters are pairwise distinct and whose tries are all valid, let $c$ be a valid trie and $a$ a letter. Then the list obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children) again has pairwise distinct letters, and every trie in it is valid.

results.title: Setting a child preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let a trie node with value $v$ and child list $L$ be valid, let $c$ be a valid trie and $a$ a letter. Then the node with value $v$ whose child list is obtained from $L$ by setting the child at $a$ to $c$ (removing the entries at $a$ instead when $c$ has neither value nor children) is valid.

results.title: Deletion from a trie
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Deleting a key $k$ (a list of letters) from a trie $t$ works by recursion on $k$. If $k$ is empty, the root of $t$ loses its value and keeps its children. If $k$ consists of a first letter $a$ followed by a key $k'$ and the root of $t$ has no child at $a$, then $t$ is unchanged. Otherwise $k'$ is deleted from the first child at $a$. results.title: A deleted key is absent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every trie $t$ and every key $k$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k$ finds no value.

results.title: Deletion does not affect other keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every trie $t$ and all keys $k \ne k'$, looking up $k$ in the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k'$ gives the same result as looking up $k$ in $t$.

results.title: Deletion preserves trie validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a trie $t$ is valid, that is, every node has distinct child keys and valid child tries, then for every key $k$ the trie obtained from $t$ by deleting $k$ is valid.

results.title: Strict preference orders for the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A strict total order on a type $\alpha$ is a binary relation $<$ on $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$). In the Gibbard–Satterthwaite development it models a voter's strict preference over alternatives.

results.title: Building a strict preference order in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A binary relation $<$ on a type $\alpha$ that is irreflexive ($a < a$ holds for no $a$), transitive ($a < b$ and $b < c$ imply $a < c$) and total on distinct elements ($a \ne b$ implies $a < b$ or $b < a$) defines a strict total order on $\alpha$ whose relation is $<$.

results.title: Relation of a strict preference order
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The relation of a strict total order $T$ on a type $\alpha$ is its underlying binary relation $\lt _T$ on $\alpha$, which is irreflexive, transitive, and relates any two distinct elements in one direction or the other.

results.title: Irreflexivity of strict preference
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $T$ be a strict total order on a type $\alpha$, with relation $\lt _T$. Then $a \lt _T a$ fails for every $a \in \alpha$.

results.title: Transitivity of strict preferences in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b, c \in \alpha$ satisfy $a < b$ and $b < c$, then $a < c$.

results.title: Strict preferences in the Gibbard–Satterthwaite setting are total
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $<$ be the relation of a strict total order on a type $\alpha$. If $a, b \in \alpha$ and $a \ne b$, then $a < b$ or $b < a$.

results.title: Preference profiles for the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a type $A$ of alternatives and a type $V$ of voters, a profile is a function assigning to each voter $i \in V$ a strict total order $\lt _i$ on $A$, the strict preference of voter $i$.

results.title: Social choice functions
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a type $A$ of alternatives and a type $V$ of voters, a resolute social choice function is a function $F$ sending each profile $p$ (an assignment of a strict total order on $A$ to each voter in $V$) to a single chosen alternative $F(p) \in A$.

results.title: Top-ranked alternative
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a strict total order $o$ on the alternatives, write $x \succ_o y$ when $x$ is related to $y$ by $o$ ($o$ ranks $x$ above $y$). An alternative $t$ is top-ranked by $o$ when $t \succ_o b$ for every alternative $b \ne t$.

results.title: Onto social choice function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A resolute social choice function $F$ is onto when every alternative $a$ is chosen at some profile, that is, $F(p) = a$ for some profile $p$.

results.title: Profiles differing only at one voter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p_1$ and $p_2$ be profiles, each assigning a strict total order on the alternatives to every voter, and let $i$ be a voter. Then $p_2$ differs from $p_1$ at most at voter $i$ when $p_1(j) = p_2(j)$ for every voter $j \ne i$.

results.title: Strategy-proof social choice function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a strict total order $P$, write $x \succ_P y$ when $x$ is related to $y$ by $P$ ($P$ ranks $x$ above $y$). A resolute social choice function $F$ is strategy-proof when, for all profiles $p_1$, $p_2$ and every voter $i$ such that $p_1(j) = p_2(j)$ for all voters $j \ne i$, it is not the case that $F(p_2) \succ_{p_1(i)} F(p_1)$: no voter gains by misreporting alone, judged by the true order $p_1(i)$.

results.title: Dictator of a social choice function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a resolute social choice function $F$, a voter $d$ is a dictator when, for every profile $p$, the chosen alternative $F(p)$ is top-ranked in the preference order $p(d)$ of voter $d$.

results.title: Dictatorial social choice function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A resolute social choice function $F$ is dictatorial when some voter is a dictator for $F$: there is a voter $d$ such that, for every profile $p$, the chosen alternative $F(p)$ is top-ranked in the preference order $p(d)$ of voter $d$.

results.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem, finiteness form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the set of alternatives be finite and the set of voters be finite and nonempty, and suppose there are at least three distinct alternatives. Then every resolute social choice function on profiles of strict preference orders that is onto and strategy-proof is dictatorial.

results.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the set of alternatives be finite and the set of voters be finite and nonempty, and suppose there are at least three distinct alternatives. Then every resolute social choice function on profiles of strict preference orders that is onto and strategy-proof is dictatorial.
